content: Grapefruit seed extract (GSE), also referred to as citrus seed extract, is a liquid derived from the seeds, pulp, and white membranes of grapefruit. Despite the lack of scientific evidence supporting its efficacy, some alternative medicine practitioners claim that GSE possesses antibacterial, antiviral, and antifungal properties. It has been recommended by certain nutritionists for conditions such as candidiasis, ear infections, throat infections, and diarrhea. Additionally, some natural food retailers promote GSE as a safe, natural, and effective preservative. Recent studies have identified synthetic preservatives in commercial GSE products. When these preservatives were absent, laboratory tests revealed that the natural extracts exhibited little to no inherent antimicrobial activity. Dr. Jacob Harich, a nuclear physicist, was an early proponent of GSE and developed it in the 1960s. He began researching and marketing GSE after moving to Florida, a major grapefruit-producing region. Today, GSE is primarily marketed through health food stores and online platforms. Anecdotal claims of GSE’s antimicrobial effects are loosely supported by small-scale in vitro experiments, such as agar diffusion tests, which suggest some antimicrobial activity. However, substantial scientific evidence indicates that the antimicrobial effects observed in commercial GSE preparations are due to contamination or adulteration with synthetic antimicrobials or preservatives. For example, a 2001 study reviewed by chemist G. Takeoka documented that commercial GSE products contained synthetic compounds like benzethonium chloride, which could not have been derived from grapefruit seeds. Despite this, proponents, including authors and cosmetic companies, continue to assert that GSE has strong natural healing properties, even though scientific studies contradict these claims. The grapefruit tree, originally referred to as the forbidden fruit of Barbados, was first documented in 1750 by Rev. Griffith Hughes. All parts of the fruit have various uses. The fruit is primarily consumed for its tangy juice, while the peel is used to produce aromatherapy oil and dietary fiber. The seeds and pulp, byproducts of the juice industry, are sold as cattle feed and used to manufacture GSE. Commercially available GSE is typically made from grapefruit seed, pulp, glycerin, and synthetic preservatives. Independent studies have shown that commercial GSE preparations often contain synthetic antimicrobial agents such as benzalkonium chloride, benzethonium chloride, triclosan, or methylparaben. Some samples have been found to contain up to 22% benzalkonium chloride by weight, a compound known for its allergenic and toxic properties at higher doses. These synthetic chemicals are not present in laboratory-prepared GSE, and pure GSE without contaminants has been found to lack significant antimicrobial effects. Self-made citrus seed extracts also do not exhibit broad-spectrum preservative capabilities. Although GSE is marketed as a powerful antimicrobial agent with proven activity against bacteria and fungi, independent studies have consistently demonstrated that its efficacy as an antimicrobial is not supported. Claims of universal antimicrobial benefits are attributed to the presence of synthetic preservatives rather than any natural properties of GSE. Furthermore, studies examining the antiviral properties of GSE found it ineffective as a disinfectant against feline calicivirus and feline parvovirus. There is evidence that grapefruit seed extract contains low levels of antioxidant properties. Analysis of its constituents reveals the presence of flavonoids, ascorbic acid (vitamin C), tocopherols, citric acid, limonoids, sterols, and minerals. Some studies suggest that the bioactive compounds in grapefruit seed and pulp may help suppress the development of colon cancer. Additionally, the flavonoid naringin has been shown to lower plasma lipid levels and elevate plasma antioxidant activity. Due to the identification of synthetic preservatives in commercial GSE products, individuals sensitive to synthetic preservatives should exercise caution when using GSE to avoid allergic reactions. Grapefruit itself is known to interact with certain medications by inhibiting the production of a specific intestinal enzyme, thereby increasing the absorption rate of several drugs. The controversy surrounding GSE persists, as it continues to be popularized by health food companies, books, and online marketers. Despite its promotion as an effective natural preservative, scientific studies have consistently concluded that the antimicrobial activity associated with GSE is due to contamination with synthetic antimicrobials, and natural GSE lacks inherent antimicrobial properties.
